title: EU AI Act Article 50(4): Deepfake Disclosure Obligations for Deployers — Council of AI Compliance Guide
context: 2026-09-01 engine cycle — Article 50(4) requires deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate content constituting a deepfake to disclose that the content is artificial. This is distinct from Art 50(2) machine-readable marking (which falls on providers) and creates a downstream liability chain. High-risk deepfake deployers face the August 2026 deadline.
body: EU AI Act Article 50(4) places the disclosure burden on deployers when they deploy an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a deepfake. The deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Three operational questions dominate. (1) What counts as a deepfake? The Act defines deepfakes as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities, or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic. Text-only generation is excluded but may fall under Art 50(1) interaction disclosure. (2) Who is a deployer? Any person or entity using an AI system under their authority, including SaaS platforms embedding GPAI models and public-sector bodies using AI in citizen-facing services. (3) What constitutes adequate disclosure? The European AI Office Code of Practice on GPAI recommends a layered approach: a human-readable label plus a machine-readable provenance assertion (C2PA 2.1 or SCITT per IETF RFC 9424) that survives content redistribution. The Council of AI verified measurement credential cryptographically binds a deployer attestation to a deployment event, timestamp, and content hash — producing a signed record that an auditor, regulator, or court can verify offline. Practitioners should treat August 2026 as go-live for high-risk deepfake deployers.
